## Appendix A Detailed Analysis

### A.1 Preliminaries on mollifiers

#### Proposition A.1.

For $s>n$ , the $s$ -Riesz family of mollifiers, defined as $\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(x):=(\norm{x}^{2}_{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{-s/2}/Z^{s}_{\epsilon}$ , satisfies Definition 3.1.

In order to prove Proposition A.1, we first prove a lemma.

#### Lemma A.2.

Let $b\geq 0$ . Then for any $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{B_{\epsilon}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(y)\norm{y}_{2}^{b}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\left(\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{n+b-1}}{(t^{2}+1)^{s/2}}\right)\epsilon^{n+b-s}, $$

where $\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})$ is the volume of the $(n-1)$ -dimensional sphere.

Furthermore, assuming $s>b+n$ , then for any $\epsilon>0,\delta>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(y)\norm{y}_{2}^{b}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\frac{\delta^{n+b-s}}{s-(n+b)}. $$

#### Proof.

For (8), we compute

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{B_{\epsilon}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(y)\norm{y}_{2}^{b}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int_{B_{\epsilon}(0)}\frac{\norm{y}_{2}^{b}}{(\norm{y}_{2}^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{s/2}}=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\int_{0}^{\epsilon}\frac{r^{n+b-1}}{(r^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{s/2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\epsilon t)^{n+b-1}}{(\epsilon^{2}t^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{s/2}}\epsilon\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\left(\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{n+b-1}}{(t^{2}+1)^{s/2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\right)\epsilon^{n+b-s}, $$

where we use substitution $r=\epsilon t$ on the second line.

If $s>b+n$ , then

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(0,y)\norm{y}_{2}^{b}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\frac{\norm{y}_{2}^{b}}{(\norm{y}_{2}^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{s/2}} \displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\frac{\norm{y}_{2}^{b}}{\norm{y}_{2}^{s}}=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\int_{\delta}^{\infty}r^{n-1+b-s} \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})\frac{\delta^{n+b-s}}{s-(n+b)}, $$

where the last integral uses $s>b+n$ . ∎

#### Proof of Proposition A.1.

It is clear that (a) of Proposition A.1 holds for $\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)$ . Since $\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)$ is bounded we have $\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . For any $\delta>0$ , we have, for $\epsilon\leq\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{B_{\delta}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\geq Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{B_{\epsilon}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=C\epsilon^{n-s}, $$

where we use (8) with $b=0$ and $C$ is a constant depending only on $n,s$ . On the other hand, using (9) with $b=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\phi^{s}_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\leq C^{\prime}\delta^{n-s}, $$

where $C^{\prime}$ depends only on $n,s$ . With $\delta=\epsilon$ , we see that $Z_{\epsilon}^{s}\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ so (b) is satisfied.

Since $\delta$ is fixed and $s>n$ , we see that

$$ \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{\int_{B_{\delta}(0)}\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x}{\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x}\geq\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{C\epsilon^{n-s}}{C^{\prime}\delta^{n-s}}=\infty. $$

Since $\int_{B_{\delta}(0)}\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x$ $+\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(0)}\phi_{\epsilon}^{s}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=1$ , we have shown (c). ∎

In the rest of this section, we assume $\{\phi_{\epsilon}\}_{\epsilon>0}$ is a family of mollifiers satisfying Definition 3.1.

#### Lemma A.3.

For any $p\in[1,\infty]$ , for any $\delta>0$ , $\phi_{\epsilon}\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ and $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n\setminus B_\delta(0)} \phi_\eps}_{p}=0$ . holds.

#### Proof.

Assume $p\notin\{1,\infty\}$ since both cases are covered in the assumptions. Then for any $\delta>0$ , by Hölder’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\norm{\phi_\eps}_{p}^{p}=\norm{\phi_\eps\cdot\phi_\eps^{p-1}}_{1}\leq\norm{\phi_\eps}_{1}\norm{\phi_\eps^{p-1}}_{\infty}=\norm{\phi_\eps}_{1}\norm{\phi_\eps}_{\infty}^{p-1}<\infty. $$

Similarly,

$$ \displaystyle\norm{\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps}_{p}^{p} \displaystyle=\norm{\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps^p}_{1}=\norm{\phi_\eps\cdot\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps^{p-1}}_{1} \displaystyle\leq\norm{\phi_\eps}_{1}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n\setminus B_\delta(0)} \phi_\eps^{p-1}}_{\infty}=\norm{\ind_{\RR^n\setminus B_\delta(0)} \phi_\eps}_{\infty}^{p-1}. $$

Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ and applying (c) gives $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n\setminus B_\delta(0)} \phi_\eps}_{p}=0$ . ∎

#### Proposition A.4.

Let $f\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $p\in[1,\infty]$ . Then for every $\epsilon>0$ , the integral

$$ \int f(x-y)\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y $$

exists, so that $(f*\phi_{\epsilon})(x)$ is finite. Moreover, if $f$ is continous at $x$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}(f*\phi_{\epsilon})(x)=f(x). $$

#### Proof.

Observe that by Hölder’s inequality, for $q$ such that $1/p+1/q=1$ (allowing infinity),

$$ \displaystyle\int\absolutevalue{f(x-y)\phi_\eps(y)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq\norm{f}_{p}\norm{\phi_\eps}_{q}<\infty. $$

Hence $(f*\phi_{\epsilon})(x)$ is integrable and finite.

For any $\epsilon>0$ , note that

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{(f * \phi_\eps)(x) - f(x)} \displaystyle=\absolutevalue{\int f(x-y)\phi_\eps(y) \dd y - f(x)}. $$

Since $\int\phi_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{(f * \phi_\eps)(x) - f(x)} \displaystyle=\absolutevalue{\int\left(f(x-y) - f(x)\right) \phi_\eps(y) \dd y}\leq\int\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y. $$

Fix $t>0$ . Continuity of $f$ at $x$ implies there exists $\delta>0$ such that $\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}<t$ for all $y\in B_{\delta}(0)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B_{\delta}(0)}\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq t\int_{B_{\delta}(0)}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq t. $$

On the other hand, by Hölder’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus B_{\delta}(x)}\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq\norm{\tau_x f - f}_{p}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps}_{q}\leq 2\norm{f}_{p}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps}_{q}. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{(f * \phi_\eps)(x) - f(x)} \displaystyle\leq t+2\norm{f}_{p}\norm{\ind_{\RR^n \setminus B_\delta(0)}\phi_\eps}_{q}. $$

By Lemma A.3, since $\norm{f}_{p}<\infty$ , taking $\epsilon\to 0$ we get, for any $t>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\limsup_{\epsilon\to 0}\absolutevalue{(f * \phi_\eps)(x) - f(x)} \displaystyle\leq t. $$

Now let $t\to 0$ we get (10). ∎

#### Corollary A.5.

Let $f\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $p\in[1,\infty]$ , be a continuous function. If $\{f_{\epsilon}\}$ is a sequence of functions that converge uniformly to $f$ , then for every $x$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}(f_{\epsilon}*\phi_{\epsilon})(x)=f(x). $$

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{(\phi_\eps* f_\eps)(x) - f(x)} \displaystyle\leq\absolutevalue{(\phi_\eps* f_\eps)(x) - (\phi_\eps* f)(x)}+\absolutevalue{(\phi_\eps* f)(x) - f(x)}. $$

Proposition A.4 shows the second term goes to $0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$ . For the first term, we have

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{(\phi_\eps* f_\eps)(x) - (\phi_\eps* f)(x)} \displaystyle=\absolutevalue{\int\left( f_\eps(x-y)-f(x-y)\right) \phi_\eps(y) \dd y} \displaystyle\leq\sup_{x}\absolutevalue{f_\eps(x) - f(x)}\to 0 $$

by uniform convergence. ∎

#### Lemma A.6.

For $f\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $p\in[1,\infty)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{y\to 0}\norm{\tau_y f - f}_{p}=0, $$

where we use $\tau_{a}f$ to denote the translated function $\tau_{a}f(x):=f(x-a)$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ . It is a standard fact that $C_{c}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is dense in $L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Hence there exists $g\in C_{c}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ such that $\norm{f - g}_{p}<\epsilon$ . Since $g$ is continuous with compact support, it is uniform continuous. Then there exists $\delta>0$ with $\absolutevalue{g(x-y) - g(x)}<\epsilon^{1/p}/\mathcal{L}_{n}(K)$ if $y\in B_{\delta}(x)$ . Hence for such $y$ we have $\norm{\tau_y g - g}^{p}_{p}<\epsilon$ with $\mathcal{L}_{n}(K)<\infty$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle\norm{\tau_y f - f}_{p} \displaystyle\leq\norm{\tau_y f - \tau_y g}_{p}+\norm{\tau_y g - g}_{p}+\norm{g - f}_{p}\leq 3\epsilon. $$

∎

#### Proposition A.7.

Let $f\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $p\in(1,\infty)$ . Then for every $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\norm{f * \phi_\eps}_{p}\leq 3\norm{f}_{p}. $$

In particular, $f*\phi_{\epsilon}\in L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\norm{f * \phi_\eps- f}_{p}=0. $$

#### Proof.

For every $\epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\norm{f * \phi_\eps- f}^{p}_{p} \displaystyle=\int\absolutevalue{ \int(f(x-y) - f(x)) \phi_\eps(y) \dd y}^{p}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle\leq\int\int\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}^{p}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle=\int\left(\int\absolutevalue{f(x-y) - f(x)}^{p}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\right)\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int\norm{\tau_y f - f}_{p}^{p}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y, $$

where we use Jensen’s inequality with the observation that $\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y$ is a probability measure and Tonelli’s theorem to exchange the order of integration. To show the first claim, note that,

$$ \displaystyle\norm{f * \phi_\eps- f}^{p}_{p}\leq\int\norm{\tau_y f - f}_{p}^{p}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq\int(2\norm{f}_{p})^{p}\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y=(2\norm{f}_{p})^{p}. $$

Hence $\norm{f * \phi_\eps}_{p}\leq\norm{f}_{p}+\norm{f * \phi_\eps- f}_{p}\leq 3\norm{f}_{p}$ .

For the second claim, by Lemma A.6, the function $y\mapsto\norm{\tau_y f - f}_{p}^{p}$ is continuous at $y=0$ with limit $0$ . Hence by Proposition A.4, we are done by taking $\epsilon\to 0$ . ∎

### A.2 Convergence to $\chi^{2}$ -divergence

We start by giving an alternative formula for $\chi^{2}$ divergence with respect to the target measure.

#### Lemma A.8.

Define a functional $\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to[0,\infty]$ by

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{E}(\mu):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\int_{X}\frac{q(x)^{2}}{p(x)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x&\text{ if }\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=q(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}_{n}(x)\text{ and $\mu\ll\mu^{*}$}\\
\infty&\text{ otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\end{split} $$

Then for every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ ,

$$ \mathcal{E}(\mu)=\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})+1. $$

#### Proof.

If $\mu$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu^{*}$ , then both sides are infinity. Otherwise, $\mu(X)=1$ and $\mu$ has some density $q$ . We then compute

$$ \displaystyle\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})+1 \displaystyle=\int\left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}}(x)-1\right)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}(x)+1=\int_{X}\left(\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}-1\right)^{2}p(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x+1 \displaystyle=\int_{X}\frac{q(x)^{2}}{p(x)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x-2\int_{X}q(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x+2=\int_{X}\frac{q(x)^{2}}{p(x)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\mathcal{E}(\mu). $$

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3.

Since $\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})<\infty$ , we know $\mu\ll\mu^{*}$ , so $\mu(X)=1$ . We let $q(x)$ be the density of $\mu$ which satisfies $q(x)=0$ for $x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}\setminus X$ . We compute using Tonelli’s theorem (since our integrand is positive):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu) \displaystyle=\iint\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)(p(x)p(y))^{-1/2}q(x)q(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\frac{q}{\sqrt{p}}\right)(x)\frac{q}{\sqrt{p}}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\int(\phi_{\epsilon}*g)(x)g(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x, $$

where we define $g(x):=q(x)/\sqrt{p(x)}$ on $X$ and $g(x):=0$ for $x\notin X$ . Moreover, by Lemma A.8,

$$ \displaystyle\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})+1=\int g(x)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x. $$

The assumption $\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})<\infty$ then implies $g\in L^{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . By Proposition A.7, we have $\phi_{\epsilon}*g\in L^{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Next notice that

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{\mathcal{E}_\eps(\mu) - \left(\chi^2\infdivx{\mu}{\mu^*} + 1\right)} \displaystyle\leq\int\absolutevalue{(\phi_\eps* g)(x) - g(x) }g(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\leq\norm{\phi_\eps* g - g}_{2}\norm{g}_{2}<\infty. $$

This shows the first claim. Finally, the last expression goes to $0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$ since $\norm{\phi_\eps* g - g}_{2}\to 0$ by Proposition A.7. ∎

#### Remark A.9.

One may ask if similar results as Theorem 3.3 for $f$ -divergences other than $\chi^{2}$ divergence can be obtained using similar techniques. We think the proof of Theorem 3.3 is highly specific to $\chi^{2}$ divergence because in (13) there are two copies of $q$ coming from the definition of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ as a double integral over $\mu$ . An $f$ -divergence between $\mu$ and $\mu^{*}$ has the form $\int_{X}f(q(x)/p(x))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}p(x)$ , and the only way to have $q^{2}$ showing up is to choose $f(x)=x^{2}$ corresponding to $\chi^{2}$ divergence.

#### Remark A.10.

It is possible to prove versions of Theorem 3.3 when $X$ has Hausdorff dimension $d<n$ : in such cases $\chi^{2}$ -divergence still makes sense as does (2). When $X$ is “flat”, i.e., with Hausdorff dimension $d$ and contained in a $d$ -dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbf{R}^{n}$ , e.g., when $X$ is defined by a set of linear inequalities, then Theorem 3.3 follows if we adapt the assumptions of Definition 3.1 and calculation in the proof of Theorem 3.3 to be in the subspace. For a general $d$ -dimensional $X$ , a similar calculation yields $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)=\int_{X}\left(\int_{X}\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\left(\frac{q}{\sqrt{p}}\right)(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{d}(y)\right)\left(\frac{q}{\sqrt{p}}\right)(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{d}(x).$ For a similar argument to go through, we will need the normalizing constant $\int_{X}\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{d}(y)$ to the same for all $x$ . This is true when $X$ is a $d$ -dimensional sphere, but for a general $X$ the last integral will depend on the base point $x$ . Proving a version of Theorem 3.3 for $X$ with Hausdorff dimension $d<n$ is an interesting future direction.

### A.3 Convexity and $\Gamma$ -convergence

We start by recalling a few definitions regarding functionals in $\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ .

#### Definition A.11.

We say a functional $\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to(-\infty,\infty]$ is proper if there exists $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ such that $\mathcal{F}(\mu)<\infty$ , and is lower semicontinuous (l.s.c.) if for any weakly convergence sequence $\mu_{k}\to\mu$ , we have $\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{F}(\mu_{k})\geq\mathcal{F}(\mu)$ .

#### Lemma A.12.

For any $\epsilon>0$ , the functional $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to(-\infty,\infty]$ is proper and l.s.c. Moreover, if $X$ is compact, the minimum $\min_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(X)}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ is attained by some measure in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ .

#### Proof.

Taking any $x\in X$ , since $\phi_{\epsilon}$ is bounded and $p(x)>0$ , we see that $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\delta_{x})<\infty$ so $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ is proper. Moreover, given weakly convergence $\mu_{k}\to\mu$ , by Portmanteau theorem and the fact that $W_{\epsilon}$ is nonnegative and l.s.c., we conclude that $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ is also l.s.c.

The set of probability distributions $\mathcal{P}(X)\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is tight by the compactness of $X$ . It is closed since if $\{\mu_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{P}(X)$ weakly converges to $\mu$ , then by Portmanteau theorem, $\mu(X)\geq\limsup\mu(X)=1$ so that $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(X)$ . Hence by Prokhorov’s theorem (Theorem 5.1.3 (Ambrosio et al., 2005)), $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is (sequentially) compact. It is then an elementary result that any l.s.c. function attains its minimum on a compact set. ∎

We next prove Proposition 3.5 regarding the convexity of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ and the uniqueness of its minimum.

#### Proof of Proposition 3.5.

Let $\mu$ be any finite signed Borel measure. The compactness assumption and the fact that $p\in C^{1}(X)$ imply $p(x)>\delta$ for any $x\in X$ for some $\delta>0$ . Hence $p(x)^{-1/2}\leq\delta^{-1/2}$ , so the weighted measure $\tilde{\mu}$ defined by $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\tilde{\mu}(x):=p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)$ is also finite. By the definition of i.s.p.d. kernels, we have $\mathcal{E}_{W_{\epsilon}}(\mu)=\mathcal{E}_{k_{\epsilon}}(\tilde{\mu})>0$ if $\tilde{\mu}$ is not the zero measure, which is equivalent to $\mu$ not being zero since $p>0$ . Thus $W_{\epsilon}$ is i.s.p.d. on $X$ . Also note that $(p(x)p(y))^{-1/2}<\delta^{-1}$ for all $x,y\in X$ , so $\mathcal{E}_{W_{\epsilon}}$ is always finite. By Lemma 1.1 of Pronzato & Zhigljavsky (2021), we conclude that $\mathcal{E}_{W_{\epsilon}}$ is strictly convex in $\mathcal{M}_{\textup{sign}}$ , the space of finite signed measures, and in particular it is convex on $\mathcal{P}(X)$ . Hence combined with the existence result from Lemma A.12 we conclude $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ attains a unique minimum in $\mathcal{P}(X)$ . ∎

Our goal in the rest of this section is to prove the $\Gamma$ -convergence of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ to $\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to[0,\infty]$ defined in (12). By Lemma A.8, we have $\mathcal{E}(\mu)=\chi^{2}(\mu\;\|\;\mu^{*})+1$ . Hence together we will have proved Theorem 3.6.

#### Definition A.13 ( $\Gamma$ -convergence).

A sequence of functionals $\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to(-\infty,\infty]$ is said to $\Gamma$ -converge to $\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to(-\infty,\infty]$ , denoted as $\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Gamma}}{{\to}}\mathcal{F}$ , if:

- (a) For any sequence $\mu_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ converging weakly to $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})\geq\mathcal{F}(\mu)$ ;

- (b) For any $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , there exists a sequence $\mu_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ converging weakly to $\mu$ with $\limsup_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})\leq\mathcal{F}(\mu)$ .

We will show $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Gamma}}{{\to}}\mathcal{E}$ using Fourier transforms and Bochner’s theorem.

#### Definition A.14 (Fourier transform).

For $f\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , its Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ is the complex-valued function defined via

$$ \hat{f}(\xi):=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x. $$

More generally, for a signed finite measure $\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{\textup{sign}}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , its Fourier transform $\hat{\mu}$ is the complex-valued function defined via

$$ \hat{\mu}(\xi):=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x). $$

This integral is always well-defined and moreover $\hat{\mu}$ is uniformly continuous; see Borodachov et al. (2019, Section 1.10).

We will prove the following weak version (under the additional assumption that a mollifier $\phi$ is integrable) of Bochner’s theorem suitable for our case. In particular we will need the Fourier inversion formula which is not given in the usual statement of Bochner’s theorem. On the other hand, we cannot directly use the Fourier inversion formula since it is not obvious how to check the integrability of $\hat{\phi}$ when $\phi$ is a mollifier.

#### Lemma A.15.

Suppose $\phi\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is even, bounded, continuous, and $k(x,y):=\phi(x-y)$ is i.s.p.d. on any compact sets. Then its Fourier transform $\hat{\phi}$ is real, nonnegative, and the following inversion formula holds:

$$ \phi(x)=\int e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\quad\text{ for all $x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is adapted from that of Varadhan (2001, Theorem 2.7) and is extended to the multi-dimensional case.

Since $\hat{\phi}(\xi):=\int e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\phi(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x$ and $\phi(x)=\phi(-x)$ , with a change of variable $x^{\prime}=-x$ , we obtain $\overline{\hat{\phi}(\xi)}=\hat{\phi}(\xi)$ , so $\hat{\phi}$ is real.

Next we show that $\hat{\phi}$ is nonnegative. For $T>0$ , we compute, for a fixed $\xi\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{T^{n}}\int_{[0,T]^{n}}\int_{[0,T]^{n}}e^{-2\pi i(t-s)\cdot\xi}\phi(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{T^{n}}\int_{[-T,T]^{n}}\left(\int_{\prod_{i}[\absolutevalue{u_i},2T-\absolutevalue{u_i}]}2^{-n}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}v\right)e^{-2\pi iu\cdot\xi}\phi(u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{T^{n}}\int_{[-T,T]^{n}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{2T-2\absolutevalue{u_i}}{2}\right)e^{-2\pi iu\cdot\xi}\phi(u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{[-T,T]^{n}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-\frac{\absolutevalue{u_i}}{T}\right)\right)e^{-2\pi iu\cdot\xi}\phi(u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u, $$

where we have used change of variable $u=t-s$ , $v=t+s$ . Since $\phi\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , by dominated convergence theorem, we have as $T\to\infty$

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}\phi(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T^{n}}\int_{[0,T]^{n}}\int_{[0,T]^{n}}e^{-2\pi i(t-s)\cdot\xi}\phi(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s. $$

For $t,s\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\real\left(e^{-2\pi i(t-s)\cdot\xi}\phi(t-s))\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\cos(2\pi t\cdot\xi)k(t,s)\cos(2\pi s\cdot\xi)+\sin(2\pi t\cdot\xi)k(t,s)\sin(2\pi s\cdot\xi). $$

For a fixed $T$ , if we define a finite measure $\mu$ as $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu=\mathbf{1}_{t\in[0,T]^{n}}\cos(2\pi t \cdot\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t$ , then $k$ being i.s.p.d. implies

$$ \iint\phi(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu=\int_{[0,T]^{n}}\int_{[0,T]^{n}}\cos(2\pi t\cdot\xi)\phi(t-s)\cos(2\pi s \cdot\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\geq 0, $$

and similarly for $\sin$ . Since $\hat{\phi}$ is real, we conclude that $\hat{\phi}$ is nonnegative.

Finally we prove Lemma A.15. For $\sigma>0$ , define $\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}(\xi):=\hat{\phi}(\xi)e^{-\sigma^{2}\norm{\xi}^{2}_{2}}$ . Since $\hat{\phi}$ is bounded (because $\phi\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ ), we see that $\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . We compute, for $x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ , using Fubini’s theorem,

$$ \displaystyle\int e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\int\hat{\phi}(\xi)e^{-\sigma^{2}\norm{\xi}^{2}_{2}}e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\int\left(\int e^{-2\pi iy\cdot\xi}\phi(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right)e^{-\sigma^{2}\norm{\xi}^{2}_{2}}e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\int\left(\int e^{-2\pi i(y-x)\cdot\xi}e^{-\sigma^{2}\norm{\xi}_{2}^{2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\right)\phi(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int(\pi/\sigma^{2})^{n/2}e^{-\pi^{2}\norm{x-y}^{2}_{2}/\sigma^{2}}\phi(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y, $$

where we use the Fourier transform formula (Borodachov et al., 2019, (4.4.1)) of the Gaussian distribution. Notice that $p_{\sigma}(y):=(\pi/\sigma^{2})^{n/2}e^{-\pi^{2}\norm{x-y}^{2}_{2}/\sigma^{2}}$ is the density of a multivariate Gaussian centered at $x$ with covariance $\sigma^{2}/(2\pi^{2})\cdot\bm{I}$ . Hence $\int e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=(p_{\sigma}*\phi)(0)$ . Since $\phi$ is bounded by assumption, with $x=0$ we find $\int\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\leq\norm{\phi}_{\infty}$ . Taking $\sigma\to 0$ , by monotone convergence theorem, we have $\int\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\leq\norm{\phi}_{\infty}$ , so together with the fact that $\hat{\phi}\geq 0$ we have $\hat{\phi}\in L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Finally, since $\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}\leq\hat{\phi}$ , by dominated convergence theorem and Proposition A.4 (note $p_{\sigma}$ is centered at $x$ ), we have

$$ \int e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=\lim_{\sigma\to 0}\int e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}_{\sigma}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=\lim_{\sigma\to 0}(p_{\sigma}*\phi)(0)=\phi(x). $$

∎

#### Proposition A.16.

Given $\phi:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to\mathbf{R}$ satisfying the assumptions of Lemma A.15, for any $\nu\in\mathcal{M}_{\textup{sign}}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\iint\phi(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(y)=\int\absolutevalue{\hat{\nu}(\xi)}^{2}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi, $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma A.15,

$$ \displaystyle\iint\phi(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(y) \displaystyle=\iint\left(\int e^{-2\pi i(x-y)\cdot\xi}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(y) \displaystyle=\int\left(\int e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(x)\right)\left(\int e^{2\pi iy\cdot\xi}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(y)\right)\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\int\hat{\nu}(\xi)\overline{\hat{\nu}(\xi)}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=\int\absolutevalue{\hat\nu(\xi)}^{2}\hat{\phi}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

where we use Fubini’s theorem (all measures are finite and $e^{-2\pi i\cdot}$ is bounded) to exchange the order of integration. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.6.

First note that Definition A.13(b) is immediate from Theorem 3.3 with $\mu_{\epsilon}=\mu$ : if $\mathcal{E}(\mu)=\infty$ , then trivially $\limsup_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)\leq\mathcal{E}(\mu)$ ; otherwise we apply Theorem 3.3. So we focus on proving criterion Definition A.13(a).

Fix a sequence $\mu_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ that converges weakly to $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , and our goal is to show $\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})\geq\mathcal{E}(\mu)$ . Without loss of generality, we may assume $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})<\infty$ for all $\epsilon>0$ (these terms have no effect in $\liminf$ ), which implies $\mu_{\epsilon}(X)=1$ . By Portmanteau’s theorem and the assumption that $X$ is closed, we have $\mu(X)\geq\limsup_{\epsilon\to 0}\mu_{\epsilon}(X)=1$ . So all of $\mu_{\epsilon}$ and $\mu$ will have support in $X$ .

For $m>0,\epsilon>0$ , define a nonnegative measure $\nu_{\epsilon,m}$ by

$$ \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon,m}(x):=h_{m}(x)p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{\epsilon}(x), $$

where $h_{m}:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to\mathbf{R}$ is a continuous monotonically decreasing cutoff function satisfying $h_{m}(x)=1$ if $\norm{x}_{2}^{2}<m$ and $h_{m}(x)=0$ if $\norm{x}_{2}^{2}>m+1$ , and that $h_{m}(x)\leq h_{m^{\prime}}(x)$ for $m<m^{\prime}$ . Then since $p>0$ is continuous, it is bounded below on any compact set in $X$ , and hence $\nu_{\epsilon,m}$ is finite. Also define, for $m>0$ , a nonnegative measure $\nu_{m}$ by

$$ \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{m}(x):=h_{m}(x)p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x), $$

which is again finite following the same reasoning.

Then for any $m>0$ , denoting $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon}(x):=p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{\epsilon}(x)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon}) \displaystyle=\iint\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon}(y) \displaystyle\geq\iint\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon,m}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon,m}(y)=\int\absolutevalue{\hat\nu_{\eps,m}(\xi)}^{2}\hat{\phi}_{\epsilon}(\xi)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi, $$

where we apply Proposition A.16 for the last equality. On the other hand, note that

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\nu}_{\epsilon,m}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu_{\epsilon,m}(x)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}h_{m}(x)p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{\epsilon}(x). $$

Since $\mu_{\epsilon}\to\mu$ weakly and the last integrand is a continuous bounded function, we have

$$ \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\hat{\nu}_{\epsilon,m}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}h_{m}(x)p^{-1/2}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=\hat{\nu}_{m}(\xi). $$

On the other hand, $\hat{\phi}_{\epsilon}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}\phi_{\epsilon}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x$ . Since by Definition 3.1, $\phi_{\epsilon}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x$ converges to $\delta_{0}$ in probability (and in particular weakly), we have $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\hat{\phi}_{\epsilon}(\xi)=1$ .

Applying Fatou’s lemma to (15), we obtain, for any $m>0$ ,

$$ \liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})\geq\int\absolutevalue{\hat\nu_m(\xi)}^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

If $\int\absolutevalue{\hat\nu_m(\xi)}^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi=\infty$ for any $m>0$ , then we are done since $\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon})=\infty$ . Otherwise, by Kühn (2016, Lemma 2.11), for every $m>0$ , $\nu_{m}$ has density in $L^{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . This imples $\mu$ has density everywhere. Suppose $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=q(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}_{n}(x)$ . By Plancherel’s theorem and the monotone convergence theorem, we have

$$ \displaystyle\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon}) \displaystyle\geq\lim_{m\to\infty}\int\absolutevalue{\hat\nu_m(\xi)}^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\xi \displaystyle=\lim_{m\to\infty}\int_{X}\left(h_{m}(x)p^{-1/2}(x)q(x)\right)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle=\int_{X}p^{-1}(x)q(x)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\mathcal{E}(\mu). $$

This completes the proof of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Gamma}}{{\to}}\mathcal{E}$ .

Now suppose $X$ is compact, and let $\mu_{\epsilon}^{*}:=\arg\min_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(X)}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)$ . To establish $\mu^{*}_{\epsilon}\to\mu^{*}$ weakly (resp. $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu^{*}_{\epsilon})=\mathcal{E}(\mu^{*})=1$ ), it suffices to show that every subsequence of $\{\mu^{*}_{\epsilon}\}$ (resp. $\{\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon}^{*})\}$ ) has a further convergence subsequence converging to $\mu^{*}$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}(\mu^{*})$ ). With a slight abuse of notation, we assume the sequence of $\epsilon$ is chosen so that $\{\mu_{\epsilon}^{*}\}$ (resp. $\{\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{\epsilon}^{*})\}$ ) is already some subsequence of the original sequence. As argued in the proof of Lemma A.12, $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is compact with respect to weak convergence. Hence $\{\mu_{\epsilon}^{*}\}$ has a weakly convergence subsequence $\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*}\to\nu$ for some $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(X)$ . The $\Gamma$ -convergence $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Gamma}}{{\to}}\mathcal{E}$ implies

$$ \displaystyle\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu^{*})\geq\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*})\geq\mathcal{E}(\nu)\geq\limsup_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\nu)\geq\limsup_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*}), $$

where we have used, for each inequality, $\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*}=\argmin_{\mathcal{P}(X)}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}$ , Definition A.13(a), the first paragraph of this proof, and again the fact that $\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*}=\argmin_{\mathcal{P}(X)}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}$ . Since $\liminf_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu^{*})=\mathcal{E}(\mu^{*})$ by Theorem 3.3, we have

$$ \mathcal{E}(\mu^{*})\geq\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*})=\mathcal{E}(\nu)\geq\mathcal{E}(\mu^{*}), $$

where the last inequality follows because $\mu^{*}$ is the minimizer of $\mathcal{E}$ . Then $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon_{k}}(\mu_{\epsilon_{k}}^{*})=\mathcal{E}(\mu^{*})=1$ . Moreover, $\chi^{2}(\nu\;\|\;\mu^{*})=0$ . This can only happen if $\nu$ and $\mu^{*}$ agree on all Borel sets, so $\nu=\mu^{*}$ . ∎

### A.4 Differential calculus of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ in $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$

#### Lemma A.17.

Let $x_{0}\in\mathbf{R}$ , $h>0$ , and $\Omega\subset\mathbf{R}^{m}$ be a compact set. Suppose $f:(x_{0}-h,x_{0}+h)\times\Omega\to\mathbf{R}$ is jointly continuous and the derivative $\partialderivative{x}f:(x_{0}-h,x_{0}+h)\times\Omega\to\mathbf{R}$ exists and is jointly continuous. Then $\int_{\Omega}f(x,\omega)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\omega$ is differentiable for $x\in(x_{0}-h,x_{0}+h)$ , and

$$ \derivative{x}\int_{\Omega}f(x,\omega)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\omega=\int_{\Omega}\partialderivative{x}f(x,\omega)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\omega $$

where the integration is with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal{L}_{m}$ on $\Omega$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $x\in(x_{0}-h,x_{0}+h)$ and let $t>0$ be small enough such that $[x-t,x+t]\subset(x_{0}-h,x_{0}+h)$ . Note that $\int_{\Omega}f(x,\omega)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\omega$ is well-defined by the dominated convergence theorem since $\sup_{x\in[x-t,x+t],\omega\in\Omega}f(x,\omega)<\infty$ and $\mathcal{L}_{m}(\Omega)<\infty$ . Define $\theta(\omega):=\sup_{x\in[x-t,x+t]}\absolutevalue{\pdv{x} f(x,\omega)}$ which is finite since $\partialderivative{x}f(x,\omega)$ is continuous, so that $\theta(\omega)\geq\partialderivative{x}\absolutevalue{f(x,\omega)}$ for all $x\in[x-t,x+t]$ and $\theta$ is integrable since $\mathcal{L}_{m}(\Omega)<\infty$ . Hence by the differentiation lemma (Klenke, 2013, Theorem 6.28) we are done. ∎

The following lemma is similar to Korba et al. (2021, Proposition 3) but with different assumptions: we do not put any integrability assumptions on $W_{\epsilon}$ , but we do restrict measures to have compact support. For a differentiable $f:\mathbf{R}^{n}\times\mathbf{R}^{n}\to\mathbf{R}$ , we use $\nabla_{1}f(x,y)$ to denote the gradient with respect to $x$ . We also use $\mathrm{H}_{1}f(x,y)$ to denote the Hessian of $f$ with respect to $x$ . We similarly denote $\nabla_{2}f(x,y)$ and $\mathrm{H}_{2}f(x,y)$ .

#### Lemma A.18.

Assume $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ has density $q\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Let $\bm{\xi}\in C(\mathbf{R}^{n};\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . Denote $\bm{s}(x,t):=x+t\bm{\xi}(x)$ . Then for all $t>0$ and all $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\derivative{t}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=2\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}(x,t),\bm{s}(y,t))\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y). $$

In particularly,

$$ \displaystyle\derivative{t}\bigg|_{t=0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=2\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y). $$

Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\derivative[2]{t}\bigg|_{t=0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=2\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}\nabla_{2}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}(y)+\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\mathrm{H}_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}(x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y). $$

#### Proof.

We compute

$$ \displaystyle\derivative{t}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=\derivative{t}\left(2\iint W_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}(x,t),\bm{s}(y,t))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y)\right). $$

Since $\mu$ has compact support and $(x,y,t)\mapsto W_{\epsilon}(\bm{s}(x,t),\bm{s}(y,t))q(x)q(y)$ is jointly continuous and its derivative with respect to $t$ is also jointly continuous, by Lemma A.17, we can push $\derivative{t}$ inside the double integral and we obtain (16). Another application of Lemma A.17 shows that if we take derivative with respect to $t$ again on (16) and evaluate at $0$ we obtain (18). ∎

#### Lemma A.19.

Let $f\in C^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , $p\in[1,\infty]$ . Assume $\phi_{\epsilon}$ has compact support for some $\epsilon>0$ . Then for all $i=1,\ldots,n$ , $\phi_{\epsilon}*f$ is differentiable and

$$ \partialderivative{x_i}(\phi_{\epsilon}*f)(x)=\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\partialderivative{x_i}f\right)(x). $$

#### Proof.

Since $\supp(\phi_{\epsilon})$ is compact and $f\in C^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is bounded on any compact set, we know $\phi_{\epsilon}*f$ is well-defined at every $x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle\partialderivative{x_i}(\phi_{\epsilon}*f)(x) \displaystyle=\partialderivative{x_i}\left(\int f(x-y)\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(?)}}{{=}}\int\partialderivative{f}{x_i}\/(x-y)\phi_{\epsilon}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y=\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\partialderivative{x_i}f\right)(x). $$

Since $\supp(\phi_{\epsilon})$ is compact and $(x,y)\mapsto f(x-y)\phi(y)$ is $C^{1}$ , by Lemma A.17 we justify the existence of the derivative and the exchange of differentiation and integration (?). ∎

#### A.4.1 Subdifferentials of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$

Recall the following notion of a “Wasserstein gradient” in $\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ from Ambrosio et al. (2005, Definition 10.1.1).

#### Definition A.20.

A vector field $\bm{w}\in L^{2}(\mu;\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is a strong Fréchet subdifferential of a functional $\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ if for all $\bm{T}\in L^{2}(\mu;\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\bm{T}_{\#}\mu)-\mathcal{F}(\mu)\geq\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}(\bm{T}(x)-x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)+o\left(\norm{\bm{T} - \bm{I}}_{L^{2}(\mu;\mathbf{R}^{n})}\right). $$

Note that we cannot apply Ambrosio et al. (2005, Lemma 10.4.1) directly to prove (4) because interaction energies cannot be written in the form of (10.4.1) in their setup.

#### Proof of Proposition 3.7.

Let $\bm{\xi}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbf{R}^{n};\mathbf{R}^{n})$ . By Lemma A.18, we have

$$ \displaystyle\derivative{t}\bigg|_{t=0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=2\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y) \displaystyle=2\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}\left(\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)(p(x)p(y))^{-1/2}\right)\right)q(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \displaystyle=2\int\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla\left(p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x), $$

where the last step follows from applying Lemma A.17 since $q$ has compact support. Now suppose $\bm{w}\in L^{2}(\mu;\mathbf{R}^{n})$ is a strong Fréchet subdifferential satisfying (19). For the sequence $\{\bm{T}_{t}\}$ , we have by definition

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu) \displaystyle\geq\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}(\bm{T}_{t}(x)-x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)+o\left(\norm{\bm{T}_t - \bm I}_{L^{2}(\mu;\mathbf{R}^{n})}\right) \displaystyle=\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}(t\bm{\xi}(x))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)+o(t). $$

Hence

$$ \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)}{t}\geq\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}\bm{\xi}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\geq\liminf_{t\uparrow 0}\frac{\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu)}{t}. $$

The previous calculation shows $\derivative{t}|_{t=0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})$ exists, and hence it is equal to $\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}\bm{\xi}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)$ . This proves for any $\bm{\xi}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}^{n};\mathbf{R}^{n})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int\bm{w}(x)^{\top}\bm{\xi}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \displaystyle=\int\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla\left(2p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x). $$

Hence we have shown (4).

Finally, we show $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\bm{w}_{\epsilon}(x)=\bm{w}_{\chi^{2}}(x)$ for $\mu$ -a.e. $x$ under the additional assumption that $\phi_{\epsilon}$ has compact support. By Ambrosio et al. (2005, Lemma 10.4.1) with $F(x,\rho(x))=\left(\frac{\rho(x)}{p(x)}-1\right)^{2}p(x)$ , we find the strong subdifferential of $\chi^{2}(\cdot\;\|\;\mu^{*})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\bm{w}_{\chi^{2},\mu}(x)=2\nabla\frac{q(x)}{p(x)},\text{ for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}. $$

To show (5), we compute, for $\mu$ -a.e. $x$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\bm{w}_{\epsilon}(x) \displaystyle=\nabla\left(p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x)\right) \displaystyle=\nabla(p(x)^{-1/2})(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x)+p(x)^{-1/2}\nabla(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x) \displaystyle=\nabla(p(x)^{-1/2})(\phi_{\epsilon}*q/\sqrt{p})(x)+p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*\nabla(q/\sqrt{p}))(x), $$

where for the last equality we have applied Lemma A.19. Now taking $\epsilon\to 0$ , by Proposition A.4 using the fact that $\supp(\phi_{\epsilon})$ is compact (so that $q/\sqrt{p}$ and $\nabla(q/\sqrt{p})$ are bounded on $x+\supp(\phi_{\epsilon})$ ), we obtain (5). ∎

#### A.4.2 Displacement convexity of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ at $\mu^{*}$ as $\epsilon\to 0$

The statement of Proposition 3.8 is similar in form as Korba et al. (2021, Corollary 4) but in our case we do not have the second term in Equation 18 vanishing and we need to take the limit $\epsilon\to 0$ . We also do not resort to RKHS theory in the proof.

#### Proof of Proposition 3.8.

By (18), we have

$$ \displaystyle\derivative[2]{t}\bigg|_{t=0}\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t}) \displaystyle=2(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}+\mathcal{G}_{\epsilon}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle F_{\epsilon} \displaystyle=\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\nabla_{1}\nabla_{2}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}(y)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}(y) \displaystyle G_{\epsilon} \displaystyle=\iint\left(\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\mathrm{H}_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}(x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu^{*}(y). $$

We tackle $F_{\epsilon}$ first. Observe that successive application of integration by parts using the fact that $\bm{\xi}$ has compact support gives

$$ \displaystyle F_{\epsilon} \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\iint\bm{\xi}_{i}(x)\partialderivative{}{x_i}{y_j}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}_{j}(y)p(x)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=-\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\iint\partialderivative{x_i}\/(\bm{\xi}_{i}(x)p(x))\partialderivative{y_j}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\bm{\xi}_{j}(y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\iint\partialderivative{x_i}\/(\bm{\xi}_{i}(x)p(x))W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\partialderivative{y_j}\/(\bm{\xi}_{j}(y)p(y))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\iint\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partialderivative{x_i}\/(\bm{\xi}_{i}(x)p(x))\right)W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\partialderivative{y_j}\/(\bm{\xi}_{j}(y)p(y))\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y. $$

If we view $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partialderivative{x_i}\/(\bm{\xi}_{i}(x)p(x))$ as the density of a signed measure (it is integrable since it has compact support), and since $W_{\epsilon}$ is i.s.p.d. on the support of $\bm{\xi}$ by Proposition 3.5(a), we see that each double integral in the last expression is non-negative. Hence $F_{\epsilon}\geq 0$ .

Next we show $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}G_{\epsilon}=0$ . Since $\mu^{*}$ has compact support, by Fubini’s theorem,

$$ \displaystyle G_{\epsilon} \displaystyle=\int\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right)\bm{\xi}(x)p(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x. $$

To expand the integral inside the Hessian operator, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right) \displaystyle=\mathrm{H}\left(p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*\sqrt{p})(x)\right). $$

First by the chain rule and Lemma A.19, we have

$$ \displaystyle\derivative{x}\left(p(x)^{-1/2}(\phi_{\epsilon}*\sqrt{p})(x)\right) \displaystyle=\derivative{x}\left(p(x)^{-1/2}\right)(\phi_{\epsilon}*\sqrt{p})+p(x)^{-1/2}\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\derivative{x}\sqrt{p}(x)\right). $$

Differentiating again while applying Lemma A.19, we obtain after rearranging terms,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right) \displaystyle=\left(\derivative[2]{x}p(x)^{-1/2}\right)(\phi_{\epsilon}*\sqrt{p})(x) \displaystyle+2\left(\derivative{x}p(x)^{-1/2}\right)\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\derivative{x}\sqrt{p}\right)(x) \displaystyle+p(x)^{-1/2}\left(\phi_{\epsilon}*\derivative[2]{x}\sqrt{p}\right)(x). $$

By Proposition A.4 and the fact that $p\in C^{2}_{c}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\derivative[2]{x}p(x)^{-1/2}\right)\sqrt{p}(x)+2\left(\derivative{x}p(x)^{-1/2}\right)\derivative{x}\sqrt{p}(x)+p(x)^{-1/2}\derivative[2]{x}\sqrt{p}(x) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\derivative[2]{x}\left(p(x)^{-1/2}\sqrt{p(x)}\right)=0. $$

Finally, we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}G_{\epsilon} \displaystyle=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right)\bm{\xi}(x)p(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle=\int\bm{\xi}(x)^{\top}\left(\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathrm{H}_{1}\left(\int W_{\epsilon}(x,y)p(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\right)\right)\bm{\xi}(x)p(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle=0, $$

where interchanging the limit and the integral is jusfitied by the dominated convergence theorem and the fact that $p$ and $\phi_{\epsilon}$ have compact support (we need compact support assumption of $\phi_{\epsilon}$ to make sure convolutions appearing in (21) are uniformly bounded when $\epsilon$ is sufficiently small).

∎

#### A.4.3 A descent lemma for $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ with time discretization

We now consider a time discretization of the gradient flow of $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ given by, for an initial measure $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ and $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$ , with a step size $\gamma>0$ ,

$$ \mu_{m+1}:=(\bm{I}-\gamma\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}})_{\#}\mu_{m}. $$

Similar to Korba et al. (2021, Proposition 14), we can show the following descent lemma for iterations (22) with the following additional assumptions:

#### Assumption A.21.

Suppose the target density $p\in C^{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ satisfies $1/C_{p}\leq p(x)\leq C_{p}$ , $\norm{p(x)}_{2}\leq C^{\prime}_{p}$ , $\norm{\hess p(x)}_{2}\leq C^{\prime\prime}_{p}$ for some $C_{p},C^{\prime}_{p},C^{\prime\prime}_{p}$ for all $x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ , where we use $\norm{A}_{2}$ to indicate the matrix spectral norm (i.e. $\norm{A}_{2}=\sigma_{\max}(A)$ ). Suppose the mollifier $\phi_{\epsilon}\in C^{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ satisfies, in addition to Definition 3.1, $\phi_{\epsilon}(x)\leq C_{\epsilon}$ , $\norm{\nabla\phi_\eps(x)}_{2}\leq C_{\epsilon}^{\prime}$ , and $\norm{\hess\phi_\eps(x)}_{2}\leq C^{\prime\prime}_{\epsilon}$ for some $C_{\epsilon}$ , $C_{\epsilon}^{\prime}$ , $C_{\epsilon}^{\prime\prime}$ .

#### Lemma A.22.

Under Assumption A.21, there exists a constant $L>0$ such that the function $\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}:\mathbf{R}^{n}\times\mathbf{R}^{n}\to\mathbf{R}^{n}$ is $L$ -Lipschitz in terms of $\norm{\cdot}_{2}$ in either input.

#### Proof.

Denote $r(x):=p(x)^{-1/2}$ . Then our assumptions imply $r(x)\leq C_{r}:=C_{p}^{1/2}$ , $\norm{\nabla r(x)}_{2}\leq C_{r}^{\prime}:=\frac{1}{2}C_{p}^{3/2}C_{p}^{\prime}$ , and $\norm{\hess_1 r(x)}_{2}\leq C_{r}^{\prime\prime}:=\frac{3}{4}C_{p}^{5/2}C_{p}^{\prime 2}+\frac{1}{2}C_{p}^{3/2}C_{p}^{\prime\prime}$ . We compute, for $x,y\in\mathbf{R}^{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y) \displaystyle=\nabla_{x}\left(\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)r(x)r(y)\right) \displaystyle=\nabla\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)r(x)r(y)+\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\nabla r(x)r(y). $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{H}_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y) \displaystyle=\mathrm{H}\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)r(x)r(y)+2\nabla\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\nabla r(x)^{\top}r(y)+\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\mathrm{H}r(x)r(y), $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{2}\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y) \displaystyle=-\mathrm{H}\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)r(x)r(y)+\nabla\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)r(x)\nabla r(y)^{\top} \displaystyle-\nabla\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\nabla r(x)r(y)+\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)\nabla r(x)\nabla r(y)^{\top}. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\norm{\hess_1 W_\eps(x,y)}_{2} \displaystyle\leq C^{\prime\prime}_{\epsilon}C_{r}^{2}+2C_{\epsilon}^{\prime}C_{r}^{\prime}C_{r}+C_{\epsilon}C_{r}^{\prime\prime}C_{r}, \displaystyle\norm{\nabla_2\nabla_1 W_\eps(x,y)}_{2} \displaystyle\leq C_{\epsilon}^{\prime\prime}C_{r}^{2}+2C_{\epsilon}^{\prime}C_{r}C_{r}^{\prime}+C_{\epsilon}C_{r}^{\prime 2}. $$

Hence we conclude that $\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}$ is $L$ -Lipschitz with

$$ L:=C^{\prime\prime}_{\epsilon}C_{r}^{2}+2C_{\epsilon}^{\prime}C_{r}^{\prime}C_{r}+C_{\epsilon}\max(C_{r}^{\prime\prime}C_{r},C_{r}^{\prime 2}). $$

∎

#### Remark A.23.

Compared with Korba et al. (2021, Lemma 1), to ensure $\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}$ is Lipscthiz, we only require uniform boundedness of $p$ and $\phi_{\epsilon}$ up to second order derivatives instead of up to order 3.

#### Proposition A.24.

Under Assumption A.21, suppose $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ has compact support. Then for any $\gamma\leq\frac{1}{2L}$ , with $L$ defined as in Lemma A.22 and $\{\mu_{m}\}_{m>0}$ defined as in (22),

$$ \mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m+1})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m})\leq-\gamma(1-2\gamma L)\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}}_{L^{2}(\mu_{m})}\leq 0. $$

#### Proof.

We first show $\mu_{m}$ has compact support for all $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . For $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{n})$ with compact support, the proof of Proposition 3.7 implies (note Proposition 3.7 assumes $\mu$ has density but it is not necessary to obtain the following formula using the same proof)

$$ \displaystyle\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu}(x)=2\int\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y). $$

Since $x\mapsto\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)$ is $C^{1}$ by the assumptions and $\mu$ has compact support, by Lemma A.17, we see that $\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu}$ is differentiable with

$$ \nabla\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu}(x)=2\int\mathrm{H}_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y). $$

By induction, suppose $\mu_{m}$ has compact support. Then

$$ \displaystyle\supp(\mu_{m+1})\subset\left(\bm{I}-\gamma\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}\right)_{\#}\supp(\mu_{m})\subset\supp(\mu_{m})+\gamma\left(\sup_{x\in\supp(\mu_{m})}\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}}_{2}\right)B_{1}(0). $$

Since $\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}$ is continuous, the set on the right-hand side is bounded. Hence $\mu_{m+1}$ has compact support.

Now fix $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$ and we show (23). Define a path $\left\{\mu_{t}\right\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ defined by $\mu_{t}=(\bm{I}-\gamma t\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}})_{\#}\mu_{m}$ . Let $f(t):=\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{t})$ . By Lemma A.18, the continuity of $\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}$ implies that $f$ is differentiable. Moreover, another application of Lemma A.17 implies that $f$ is twice differentiable, and in particular continuously differentiable. Hence $f$ is absolutely continuous on the compact interval $[0,1]$ . By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m+1})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m}) \displaystyle=f(1)-f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)+\int_{0}^{1}(f^{\prime}(t)-f^{\prime}(0))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t. $$

Observe that by Lemma A.18,

$$ \displaystyle f^{\prime}(0) \displaystyle=2\iint(-\gamma\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}(x))^{\top}\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(y) \displaystyle=\int(-\gamma\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}(x))\left(2\int\nabla_{1}W_{\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(y)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x) \displaystyle=-\gamma\norm{\bm w_{\eps, \mu_m}(x)}^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu_{m})}, $$

where we apply Fubini’s theorem to exchange the order of integration together with the fact that $\mu_{m}$ has compact support and the integrand is continuous. Let $\bm{s}(x,t):=x-\gamma t\bm{w}_{\epsilon,\mu_{m}}(x)$ . Note that, again by Lemma A.18,

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{f'(t) - f'(0)} \displaystyle\leq 2\iint\absolutevalue{(-\gamma\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(x))^\top\left(\nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x,t),\bm s(y,t)) - \nabla_1 W_\eps(x,y) \right)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(y) \displaystyle\leq 2\gamma\iint\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(x)}_{2}\norm{\nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x,t), \bm s(y, t)) - \nabla_1 W_\eps(x,y)}_{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(y). $$

Note that, by Lemma A.22, we have

$$ \displaystyle\norm{\nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x,t), \bm s(y, t)) - \nabla_1 W_\eps(x,y)}_{2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\norm{\nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x, t), \bm s(y, t)) - \nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x, t), y)}_{2}+\norm{\nabla_1 W_\eps(\bm s(x, t), y) - \nabla_1 W_\eps(x, y)}_{2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle L\gamma t(\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(x)}_{2}+\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(y)}_{2}). $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\absolutevalue{f'(t) - f'(0)} \displaystyle\leq 2\gamma^{2}Lt\iint\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(x)}_{2}\left(\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(x)}_{2}+\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}(y)}_{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(y) \displaystyle\leq 2\gamma^{2}Lt\left(\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}}_{L^{2}(\mu_{m})}+\left(\int\norm{\bm w_{\eps, \mu_m}(x)}_{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{m}(x)\right)^{2}\right) \displaystyle\leq 4\gamma^{2}Lt\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}}_{L^{2}(\mu_{m})}, $$

where we have used the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality in the last step.

Combining everything, we have shown

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m+1})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\mu_{m}) \displaystyle=f^{\prime}(0)+\int_{0}^{1}(f^{\prime}(t)-f^{\prime}(0))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle\leq-\gamma(1-2\gamma L)\norm{\bm w_{\eps,\mu_m}}_{L^{2}(\mu_{m})}\leq 0, $$

since $\gamma<\frac{1}{2L}$ .

∎

## Appendix B Weighted hypersingular Riesz energy

We recall results most relevant to us from Borodachov et al. (2019). Suppose $X\subset\mathbf{R}^{n}$ is compact, of Hausdorff dimension $d$ , and $d$ -rectifiable, i.e., the image of a bounded set in $\mathbf{R}^{d}$ under a Lipschitz mapping. Given a non-vanishing continuous probability density $p$ on $X$ , define a measure $\mathcal{H}_{d}^{p}(B):=\int_{B}p(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{d}(x)$ for any Borel set $B\subset X$ . The target measure $h_{d}^{p}$ is defined to be $h_{d}^{p}(B):=\nicefrac{{\mathcal{H}_{d}^{p}(B)}}{{\mathcal{H}_{d}^{p}(X)}}$ . The weighted $s$ -Riesz energy is defined as the interaction energy

$$ \displaystyle E_{s}(\omega_{N}):=\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{(p(x_{i})p(x_{j}))^{-s/2d}}{\norm{x_i-x_j}^{s}}. $$

The following result states that minimizers of the weighted $s$ -Riesz energy approximate the target measure when the $s$ is sufficiently large.

#### Theorem B.1 (Theorem 11.1.2, Borodachov et al. (2019)).

Suppose $s>d$ . For $\omega_{N}^{*}\in\argmin E_{s}$ with $\omega_{N}^{*}=\{x_{1}^{N},\ldots,x_{N}^{N}\}$ , we have weak convergence $\delta_{\omega_{N}^{*}}\to h_{d}^{p}$ as $N\to\infty$ .

A similar result with a slightly different assumption holds for $s=d$ (Theorem 11.1.3 of Borodachov et al. (2019)).

#### Comparison of (24) with discretized MIE (6).

Our theory is only valid for the full-dimensional case, i.e., $n=d$ (see a few exceptions discussed in Remark A.10). When this is the case and if the mollifier is taken to be from the $s$ -Riesz family, (6) becomes, for $s>n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle E_{\epsilon}(\omega_{N}):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\frac{(p(x_{i})p(x_{j}))^{-1/2}}{\left(\norm{x_i-x_j}^{2}_{2}+\epsilon^{2}\right)^{s/2}}. $$

Compared with (24), in our case there is an $\epsilon$ in the denominator, so that the continuous version of the energy $\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}$ does not blow up all the time (this is in contrast with the continuous version of (24)—see Borodachov et al. (2019, Theorem 4.3.1)). Moreover, the exponential scaling on $p$ is different: in our case we use $-1/2$ whereas in (24) it is $-s/2n$ . The diagonal $i=j$ is included in our energy, but this is inconsequential as another valid discretization is to discard the diagonal term (Borodachov et al., 2019, Theorem 4.2.2). On the other hand, our theory allows a bigger class of mollifiers that are not necessarily of Riesz families. We also allow $X$ to be non-compact. An interesting future research direction is to extend our theory to cases where $d<n$ , e.g., when $X$ is an embedded $d$ -dimensional submanifold in $\mathbf{R}^{n}$ .

## Appendix C Algorithmic details

In this section we provide algorithmic details of MIED and compare with the updates of SVGD (Liu & Wang, 2016). The negative gradient of (7) with respect to $x_{i}$ is

$$ \displaystyle-\nabla_{x_{i}}\log E_{\epsilon}(\omega_{N})= \displaystyle 2\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{e^{I_{ij}}}{\sum_{i,j}e^{I_{ij}}}\left((\nabla\log\phi_{\epsilon})(x_{j}-x_{i})+\frac{1}{2}\nabla\log p(x_{i})\right) \displaystyle+\frac{e^{I_{ii}}}{\sum_{i,j}e^{I_{ij}}}\nabla\log p(x_{i}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{e^{I_{ij}}}{\sum_{i,j}e^{I_{ij}}}\left(2\nabla\log\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})+\nabla\log p(x_{i})\right), $$

where

$$ I_{ij}:=\log\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{i}-x_{j})-\frac{1}{2}(\log p(x_{i})+\log p(x_{j})), $$

and to get the last equality we used the fact that $\nabla\phi(0)=0$ thanks to the assumption $\phi(x)=\phi(-x)$ . Then gradient descent on (7) gives our algorithm (Algorithm 1). The special treatment of the diagonal terms described in Section 4 amounts to modifying only the diagonal $I_{ii}$ .

```
Input : target density $p$ , mollifier $\phi_{\epsilon}$ , initial particles $\{x^{0}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ , learning rate $\eta$ , total steps $T$ .
for $t\leftarrow 1$ to $T$ do
for $i\leftarrow 1$ to $N$ do
$x^{t+1}_{i}\leftarrow x_{i}^{t}+\eta\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{e^{I_{ij}}}{\sum_{i,j}e^{I_{ij}}}\left(2\nabla\log\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})+\nabla\log p(x_{i})\right)$ , where $I_{ij}$ is defined in (25);
end for
end for
return final particles $\{x_{i}^{T}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ .
```

### C.1 Comparison with SVGD

The update formula in Algorithm 1 is similar to the one in SVGD: if we use $\phi_{\epsilon}(x-y)$ in place of the kernel $k(x,y)$ in the SVGD update and rewrite:

$$ \displaystyle x^{t+1}_{i} \displaystyle=x_{i}^{t}+\eta\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left(\nabla\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})+\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})\nabla\log p(x_{j})\right) \displaystyle=x_{i}^{t}+\eta\sum_{j=1}^{N}\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})\left(\nabla\log\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})+\nabla\log p(x_{j})\right). $$

For both algorithms, the update formula for each particle consists of attraction and repulsion terms and the total time complexity of each update iteration is $O(N^{2})$ . We note the following differences. First, in our formulation we have scaling factors $\frac{e^{I_{ij}}}{\sum_{i,j}e^{I_{ij}}}$ which help stabilizing the optimization (as a by-product of working in the logarithmic domain) and put more weight on nearby particles as well as particles in low-density regions, whereas in (SVGD) the scaling factors are $\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})$ which are not adapted to prioritize low-density regions. Second, in MIED, the attraction force for particle $i$ only comes from $\nabla\log p(x_{i})$ , whereas in (SVGD) the attraction force comes from $\nabla\log p(x_{j})$ for all $j$ ’s. Third, for each $j$ , in our formulation the repulsive force has an additional factor of $2$ in front of $\nabla\log\phi_{\epsilon}(x_{j}-x_{i})$ .

Empirically, the additional scaling factors in MIED help produce samples with good separations compared to SVGD, since closer pairs of points will have large weights. Additionally, since MIED optimizes a finite-dimensional objective (7), we can employ accelerated gradient-based optimizers like Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014), which we used in our experiments. In contrast, SVGD does not optimize any finite-dimensional objective. While practical SVGD implementations also use optimizers like Adam, it is unclear how the resulting particle dynamics is related to the gradient flow of KL divergence.

### C.2 Handling constraints with dynamic barrier method

The dynamic barrier method is introduced in Gong & Liu (2021) which solves $\min_{x}f(x)$ subject to $g(x)\leq 0$ where $g$ is scalar-valued. Intuitively, their method computes update directions by either decreasing $g(x)$ when $g(x)>0$ , following $-\nabla f(x)$ if the constraints are satisfied, or balancing both gradient directions.

In order to handle multiple constraints such as in Figure 11, we consider a generalized version of their dynamic barrier method. In this generalized setting, $g:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to\mathbf{R}^{m}$ is vector-valued and constraints are $g(x)\leq 0$ where the $\leq$ sign is interpreted coordinate wise.. Suppose we are at iteration $t$ with current solution $x^{t}$ . Then the next update direction $v^{*}$ is taken to be the $\argmin$ of

$$ \displaystyle\min_{v\in\mathbf{R}^{n}}\norm{v - \nabla f(x^t)}_{2}^{2}\text{ s.t. }\forall i=1,\ldots,m,\nabla g_{i}(x^{t})^{\top}v\geq\alpha_{i}g_{i}(x^{t}), $$

where $\alpha_{i}>0$ are fixed hyperparameters; in our implementation we simply choose $\alpha_{i}=1$ . Then $x^{t+1}=x^{t}-\eta v^{*}$ with learning rate $\eta$ . In our implementation we use Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014) that modulates the update directions. Observe that the optimization problem (26) is the same as projecting a point $\nabla f(x^{t})$ onto the polyhedron formed by the intersection of the halfspaces $\cap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{n}:\nabla g_{i}(x^{t})^{\top}v\geq\alpha_{i}g_{i}(x^{t})\}$ . To solve (26), we use Dykstra’s algorithm (Tibshirani, 2017) which can be interpreted as running coordinate descent on the dual of (26). We use a fixed number of $20$ iterations for the Dykstra’s algorithm which we found to be sufficient for our experiments; in the case of a single constraint, we only need to use one iteration.

### D.2 Collapsed samples when the kernel width is too big

In Figure 3, we see that samples from SVGD collapse with an adaptive kernel where the variance is taken to be half of the median of the squared distance among all pairs of points (Liu & Wang, 2016); at termination the median of the squared distance is greater than $1$ in that experiment. Here we investigate this issue further. In Figure 6, for the same uniform sampling setup, we visualize the results of SVGD with a fixed kernel width and MIED with Gaussian mollifiers with the same kernel width: when the kernel width (i.e. $2\epsilon^{2}$ in $\phi^{g}_{\epsilon}(x)=\exp(-\frac{\norm{x}_2^2}{2\eps^2})/Z_{\epsilon}^{g}$ ) is too big, both SVGD and MIED result in collapsed samples. This is because since the target density is a constant, the only force in the updates is the repulsive force. When the kernel width is too large, the repulsive force coming from points in the same collapsed cluster is dominated by the repulsive force coming from points from other clusters—this is evident in the update directions shown in the leftmost column of Figure 6 (SVGD with kernel width $0.1$ ).

# Debiased Distribution Compression

**Authors:** Lingxiao Li Affiliation: MIT CSAIL Correspondence to: lingxiao@mit.edu Raaz Dwivedi Affiliation: Cornell Tech Correspondence to: dwivedi@cornell.edu Lester Mackey Affiliation: Microsoft Research New England Correspondence to: lmackey@microsoft.com

## Abstract

Modern compression methods can summarize a target distribution $\mathbb{P}$ more succinctly than i.i.d. sampling but require access to a low-bias input sequence like a Markov chain converging quickly to $\mathbb{P}$ . We introduce a new suite of compression methods suitable for compression with biased input sequences. Given $n$ points targeting the wrong distribution and quadratic time, Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT) returns $\sqrt{n}$ equal-weighted points with $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to $\mathbb{P}$ . For larger-scale compression tasks, Low-rank SKT achieves the same feat in sub-quadratic time using an adaptive low-rank debiasing procedure that may be of independent interest. For downstream tasks that support simplex or constant-preserving weights, Stein Recombination and Stein Cholesky achieve even greater parsimony, matching the guarantees of SKT with as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ weighted points. Underlying these advances are new guarantees for the quality of simplex-weighted coresets, the spectral decay of kernel matrices, and the covering numbers of Stein kernel Hilbert spaces. In our experiments, our techniques provide succinct and accurate posterior summaries while overcoming biases due to burn-in, approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo, and tempering.

Distribution compression is the problem of summarizing a target probability distribution $\mathbb{P}$ with a small set of representative points. Such compact summaries are particularly valuable for tasks that incur substantial downstream computation costs per summary point, like organ and tissue modeling in which each simulation consumes thousands of CPU hours (Niederer et al., 2011).

Remarkably, modern compression methods can summarize a distribution more succinctly than i.i.d. sampling. For example, kernel thinning (KT) (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021; Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022), Compress++ (Shetty et al., 2022), recombination (Hayakawa et al., 2023), and randomly pivoted Cholesky (Epperly and Moreno, 2024) all provide $\widetilde{O}(1/m)$ approximation error using $m$ points, a significant improvement over the $\Omega(1/\sqrt{m})$ approximation provided by i.i.d. sampling from $\mathbb{P}$ . However, each of these constructions relies on access to an accurate input sequence, like an i.i.d. sample from $\mathbb{P}$ or a Markov chain converging quickly to $\mathbb{P}$ .

Much more commonly, one only has access to $n$ biased sample points approximating a distribution $\mathbb{Q}\neq\mathbb{P}$ . Such biases are a common occurrence in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)-based inference due to tempering (Gramacy et al., 2010, where one targets a less peaked and more dispersed distribution to achieve faster convergence,), burn-in (Cowles and Carlin, 1996, where the initial state of a Markov chain biases the distribution of chain iterates,), or approximate MCMC (Ahn et al., 2012, where one runs a cheaper approximate Markov chain to avoid the prohibitive costs of an exact MCMC algorithm, e.g.,). The Stein thinning (ST) method of Riabiz et al. (2022) was developed to provide accurate compression even when the input sample sequence provides a poor approximation to the target. ST operates by greedily thinning the input sample to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy (Gretton et al., 2012, MMD,) to $\mathbb{P}$ . However, ST is only known to provide an $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ approximation to $\mathbb{P}$ ; this guarantee is no better than that of i.i.d. sampling and a far cry from the $\widetilde{O}(1/m)$ error achieved with unbiased coreset constructions.

In this work, we address this deficit by developing new, efficient coreset constructions that provably yield better-than-i.i.d. error even when the input sample is biased. For $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , our primary contributions are fourfold and summarized in Tab. 1. First, for the task of equal-weighted compression, we introduce Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT, Alg. 1), a strategy that combines the greedy bias correction properties of ST with the unbiased compression of KT to produce $\sqrt{n}$ summary points with error $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ in $O(n^{2})$ time. In contrast, ST would require $\Omega(n)$ points to guarantee this error. Second, for larger-scale compression problems, we propose Low-rank SKT (Alg. 3), a strategy that combines the scalable summarization of Compress++ with a new low-rank debiasing procedure (Alg. 2) to match the SKT guarantees in sub-quadratic $o(n^{2})$ time.

Third, for the task of simplex-weighted compression, in which summary points are accompanied by weights in the simplex, we propose greedy and low-rank Stein Recombination (Alg. 5) constructions that match the guarantees of SKT with as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ points. Finally, for the task of constant-preserving compression, in which summary points are accompanied by real-valued weights summing to $1$ , we introduce greedy and low-rank Stein Cholesky (Alg. 7) constructions that again match the guarantees of SKT using as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ points.

Underlying these advances are new guarantees for the quality of simplex-weighted coresets (Thms. 1 and 2), the spectral decay of kernel matrices (Cor. B.1), and the covering numbers of Stein kernel Hilbert spaces (Prop. 1) that may be of independent interest. In Sec. 5, we employ our new procedures to produce compact summaries of complex target distributions given input points biased by burn-in, approximate MCMC, or tempering.
